## Four households, two regions

Open 03_summaries.ipynb. All amounts are synthetic EUR per month.

```{.python}
import pandas as pd
small = pd.DataFrame({
    "id": ["A", "B", "C", "D"],
    "code": ["N", "N", "S", "S"],
    "income": [1000, 3000, 2000, 4000],
    "saving": [-100, 600, 400, 600],
})
print(small.to_string(index=False))
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
id code  income  saving
 A    N    1000    -100
 B    N    3000     600
 C    S    2000     400
 D    S    4000     600
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 01:00–03:00 (2 minutes). Ask for the mean saving before showing any groupby syntax. These four records stay visible in the notebook.
:::

## One column, three summaries

Mean saving is 375 EUR per household. Total saving is 1500 EUR.

```{.python}
print("Mean:", small["saving"].mean())
print("Median:", small["saving"].median())
print("Total:", small["saving"].sum())
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
Mean: 375.0
Median: 500.0
Total: 1500
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 03:00–05:00 (2 minutes). Calculate -100+600+400+600 by hand. The median is the average of the two middle sorted values, 400 and 600.
:::

## Several operations with agg

The list selects operations. The columns select variables.

```{.python}
totals = small[["income", "saving"]].agg(
    ["mean", "median", "sum"]
)
print(totals.to_string())
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
         income  saving
mean     2500.0   375.0
median   2500.0   500.0
sum     10000.0  1500.0
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 05:00–07:00 (2 minutes). Point to agg, then the list of function names. Contrast the different units of mean and sum. Reference: https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.agg.html
:::

## A mean within each region

Each region becomes one row in the result.

```{.python}
regional = small.groupby(
    "code", as_index=False
)["saving"].mean()
print(regional.to_string(index=False))
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
code  saving
   N   250.0
   S   500.0
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 07:00–09:00 (2 minutes). Walk through N -> two rows -> one mean. as_index=False keeps code as an ordinary column. Reference: https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/getting_started/intro_tutorials/06_calculate_statistics.html
:::

## The calculation behind groupby

North: (-100 + 600) / 2. South: (400 + 600) / 2.

```{.python}
north = small.loc[small["code"] == "N", "saving"]
south = small.loc[small["code"] == "S", "saving"]
print("North:", north.tolist(), north.mean())
print("South:", south.tolist(), south.mean())
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
North: [-100, 600] 250.0
South: [400, 600] 500.0
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 09:00–11:00 (2 minutes). Students connect the new method to filtering learned in Lecture 7. groupby repeats the same operation over all groups.
:::

## Names for the output columns

Each pair gives the input column and the operation.

```{.python}
regional = small.groupby("code", as_index=False).agg(
    households=("id", "size"),
    mean_saving=("saving", "mean"),
    total_saving=("saving", "sum"),
)
print(regional.to_string(index=False))
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
code  households  mean_saving  total_saving
   N           2        250.0           500
   S           2        500.0          1000
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 11:00–14:00 (3 minutes). Read one named aggregation slowly. households is the new column, id is the input column, size counts the rows.
:::

## The summary is another DataFrame

You can select, calculate, sort, or plot the result.

```{.python}
print(regional.columns.tolist())
print(regional["mean_saving"].tolist())
print(regional["households"].sum())
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
['code', 'households', 'mean_saving', 'total_saving']
[250.0, 500.0]
4
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 14:00–15:00 (1 minutes). This removes the common impression that a grouped result is only a printed display. The household counts should sum to the four source rows.
:::

## Sort the regional comparison

South appears first because its mean saving is larger.

```{.python}
ranked = regional.sort_values(
    "mean_saving", ascending=False
)
print(ranked[["code", "mean_saving"]].to_string(
    index=False
))
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
code  mean_saving
   S        500.0
   N        250.0
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 15:00–17:00 (2 minutes). The underlying observations stay unchanged. Ask which argument would reverse the order.
:::

## Rows and observed values

size counts rows. count counts non-missing values in its input column.

```{.python}
observed = small.copy()
observed.loc[0, "saving"] = float("nan")
counts = observed.groupby("code", as_index=False).agg(
    rows=("id", "size"),
    saving_values=("saving", "count"),
)
print(counts.to_string(index=False))
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
code  rows  saving_values
   N     2              1
   S     2              2
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 17:00–20:00 (3 minutes). There are still two northern households, but only one observed saving. Missing values can make the denominator differ between columns.
:::

## A comparison creates a Boolean column

True contributes 1 and False contributes 0 to the sum.

```{.python}
small["shortfall"] = small["saving"] < 0
print(small[["id", "saving", "shortfall"]].to_string(
    index=False
))
print("Shortfalls:", small["shortfall"].sum())
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
id  saving  shortfall
 A    -100       True
 B     600      False
 C     400      False
 D     600      False
Shortfalls: 1
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 20:00–22:00 (2 minutes). Students already know Boolean comparisons from Day 1. Here pandas applies it to every row.
:::

## A Boolean mean is a proportion

One of two northern households has negative saving: 1 / 2 = 0.5.

```{.python}
rates = small.groupby("code", as_index=False).agg(
    households=("id", "size"),
    shortfall_rate=("shortfall", "mean"),
)
print(rates.to_string(index=False))
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
code  households  shortfall_rate
   N           2             0.5
   S           2             0.0
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 22:00–24:00 (2 minutes). The percentage is 50%, not 0.5%. Students explain the southern zero using the original rows.
:::

## Exercise 1: worked answer

::: {.answer}
The median combines the middle values within each region.
:::

```{.python}
answer = small.groupby("code", as_index=False).agg(
    households=("id", "size"),
    median_saving=("saving", "median"),
    mean_rate=("saving_rate", "mean"),
)
answer = answer.sort_values("median_saving", ascending=False)
print(answer.round(3).to_string(index=False))
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
code  households  median_saving  mean_rate
   S           2          500.0      0.175
   N           2          250.0      0.050
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 29:00–32:00 (3 minutes). Ask a student to explain why North's mean rate is0.05: (-0.1+0.2)/2. Mean rate and median amount answer different questions.
:::

## A small denominator example

The households save 20% and 10% of their incomes.

```{.python}
two = pd.DataFrame({
    "income": [1000, 3000],
    "saving": [200, 300],
})
two["rate"] = two["saving"] / two["income"]
print(two.to_string(index=False))
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
 income  saving  rate
   1000     200   0.2
   3000     300   0.1
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 32:00–34:00 (2 minutes). Both incomes are positive, so the contrast here comes entirely from weighting. Use this tiny example before discussing the larger sample.
:::

## Mean rate and pooled rate

15% gives equal weight to households. 12.5% divides combined saving by combined income.

```{.python}
mean_rate = two["rate"].mean()
pooled_rate = two["saving"].sum() / two["income"].sum()
print(f"Mean household rate: {mean_rate:.1%}")
print(f"Pooled saving rate:  {pooled_rate:.1%}")
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
Mean household rate: 15.0%
Pooled saving rate:  12.5%
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 34:00–37:00 (3 minutes). Calculate 500/4000 by hand. The pooled rate gives more influence to the higher-income household. The rate must match the research question.
:::

## A separate table of region names

The shared code connects each household to one region name.

```{.python}
names = pd.DataFrame({
    "code": ["N", "S"],
    "region": ["North", "South"],
})
print(names.to_string(index=False))
print("Unique codes:", names["code"].is_unique)
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
code region
   N  North
   S  South
Unique codes: True
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 37:00–39:00 (2 minutes). Use the two tables side by side in the notebook. The lookup has one row per region code.
:::

## A left join keeps the household rows

Many households match one row in the region table.

```{.python}
joined = small.merge(
    names, on="code", how="left",
    validate="many_to_one",
)
print(joined[["id", "code", "region"]].to_string(
    index=False
))
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
id code region
 A    N  North
 B    N  North
 C    S  South
 D    S  South
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 39:00–42:00 (3 minutes). Point out that on specifies the shared key. Left means preserve the household rows. validate checks the intended relationship. Reference: https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/merging.html
:::

## A duplicated lookup row multiplies data

Both northern households now match two lookup rows.

```{.python}
bad_names = pd.concat(
    [names, names.iloc[[0]]], ignore_index=True
)
unchecked = small.merge(bad_names, on="code", how="left")
print("Households:", len(small))
print("Joined rows:", len(unchecked))
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
Households: 4
Joined rows: 6
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 42:00–44:00 (2 minutes). Ask which rows duplicate and why the join still runs. A plausible regional mean can conceal row multiplication.
:::

## Validation catches the duplicate key

The error stops us from using the six-row result.

```{.python}
try:
    small.merge(
        bad_names, on="code", how="left",
        validate="many_to_one",
    )
except pd.errors.MergeError as error:
    print(type(error).__name__)
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
MergeError
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 44:00–46:00 (2 minutes). The try/except structure only keeps the demonstration runnable. Students do not need to memorize exception handling. The important argument is validate.
:::

## An unmatched code remains visible

The left join retains household A. Its missing region exposes the unmatched code.

```{.python}
unknown = small.copy()
unknown.loc[0, "code"] = "X"
joined = unknown.merge(names, on="code", how="left")
missing = joined.loc[joined["region"].isna(), ["id", "code"]]
print(missing.to_string(index=False))
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
id code
 A    X
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 46:00–48:00 (2 minutes). Contrast unmatched keys with duplicate keys. validate checks cardinality, while isna checks whether the lookup covered every code.
:::

The helper repeats Lecture 8's preparation and adds the region names.

```{.python}
from lesson_data import load_households
df = load_households()
print("Households:", len(df))
print("Defined saving shares:", df["saving_share"].count())
print(df[["region", "saving"]].head(3).to_string(index=False))
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
Households: 195
Defined saving shares: 193
region  saving
 North  -100.0
 South   376.0
  East   814.0
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 48:00–50:00 (2 minutes). All195 households have defined saving amounts. Two zero-income households have undefined saving shares. They remain in the amount analysis.

## A summary of 195 households

Each regional count contributes to the full sample of 195 households.

```{.python}
summary = df.groupby("region", as_index=False).agg(
    households=("household_id", "size"),
    mean_saving=("saving", "mean"),
    median_saving=("saving", "median"),
)
print(summary.round(1).to_string(index=False))
assert summary["households"].sum() == len(df)
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
region  households  mean_saving  median_saving
  East          49        351.8          366.0
 North          50        223.1          171.0
 South          49        351.0          212.0
  West          47        274.9          109.0
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 50:00–52:00 (2 minutes). Have students identify the highest mean and highest median before sorting. These synthetic comparisons have no population interpretation.
:::

## Exercise 2: combine two summaries

::: {.exercise}
Return four rows. Check that the household counts still sum to 195.
:::

```{.python}
df["shortfall"] = df["saving"] < 0
# Build one table: region, households, mean_saving.
# Build another: region, shortfall_rate.
# Join them on region, using validate="one_to_one".
# Sort by shortfall_rate, largest first.
```

::: {.notes}
Clock 52:00–57:00 (5 minutes). Allow four minutes for independent coding and a minute to compare the joined table. Use groupby named aggregation as the first step.
:::

## Exercise 2: worked answer

::: {.answer}
One-to-one checks that each region appears once in each summary.
:::

```{.python}
rates = df.groupby("region", as_index=False).agg(
    shortfall_rate=("shortfall", "mean"),
)
report = summary.merge(
    rates, on="region", how="left", validate="one_to_one"
).sort_values("shortfall_rate", ascending=False)
columns = ["region", "households", "mean_saving", "shortfall_rate"]
print(report[columns].round(3).to_string(index=False))
assert report["households"].sum() == len(df)
```

::: {.terminal-output .fragment}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
region  households  mean_saving  shortfall_rate
  West          47      274.915           0.383
 North          50      223.120           0.300
  East          49      351.837           0.245
 South          49      351.041           0.245
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 57:00–60:00 (3 minutes). The joined table combines results without changing the household sample. Have students account for every region and explain each denominator.
:::
